title: Anthropic’s boss says buying compute is his hardest call, days before the IPO. Japan finds about 1,000 servers behind AI-driven attacks. IBM trains small models to ignore orders hidden in documents. llama.cpp reaches 1.0, and OpenAI folds its robotics team into its main labs.
summary: Speaking with JPMorgan’s Jamie Dimon on 13 November, Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei called compute “the deepest business dilemma” his company faces: it has to be bought a year or two ahead, and Anthropic deliberately buys on the low side and tops up on the spot market. Bloomberg puts its commitments at nearly $901 billion, about $71 billion of it due by September 2027, and says banks have turned away orders for the IPO from mainland China and Hong Kong. On 14 November Kyodo reported that a JPCERT/CC-led investigation found around 1,000 servers likely used as bases for AI-driven cyberattacks since October. IBM released two experimental Granite 4.1 models that mark instructions and data with reserved tokens, and says they resist hidden prompt injections far better than the models it tested. llama.cpp, the open-source engine for running models on your own hardware, reached version 1.0 with a promise not to break its API outside major versions. OpenAI confirmed to Fortune that it has moved its robotics researchers into its main research and applied teams.
uncertainty: Amodei’s comments come from a JPMorgan event as reported by Bloomberg and others; the commitment and IPO figures are from Anthropic’s filings as reported, and IPO details can change before pricing. The China and Hong Kong order restrictions come from unnamed people quoted by Bloomberg. The JPCERT/CC findings are from a Kyodo report; the server count is approximate and the report does not say how much of each attack AI carried out. IBM’s injection results are its own, on static benchmarks, and IBM says the models are not for production. OpenAI’s robotics change is from Fortune, confirmed by OpenAI; the 74.8% figure is from a simulation, not real robots.

stories.theme: Anthropic’s chief executive says buying compute is the company’s hardest call, and that it deliberately buys on the low side
stories.changed: On Friday 13 November 2026, at a JPMorgan Chase investor event in New York, Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei told JPMorgan’s Jamie Dimon that “compute is the deepest business dilemma that the company faces.” Compute has to be bought one to two years ahead, before anyone knows whether revenue will justify it. Buy too little and Anthropic cannot serve customers or build new technology; buy too much and “you can financially overextend yourself.” He said Anthropic buys relatively little up front and turns to the spot market for more if business goes better than expected, and compared that to buying insurance. Bloomberg puts Anthropic’s commitments at nearly $901 billion, mostly compute and chips, with about $71 billion due by September 2027. The IPO aims to raise up to $64.4 billion by selling 825 million shares at $70 to $78, with trading expected on Nasdaq on 19 November under the symbol ANT. Bloomberg also reported the offering was about six times oversubscribed, and that several banks have refused or discouraged orders from institutional investors in mainland China and Hong Kong, partly citing US arms-export rules (ITAR).
stories.matters: The maker of Claude is telling investors, in plain words, that its capacity is planned on the cautious side. If demand runs ahead of that plan, customers feel it first as limits and slowdowns.
stories.imply: Do not assume any single AI provider can always give you more capacity on demand. Do not read strong IPO demand as a verdict on whether the compute bet pays off. Amodei himself says nobody knows yet.
uses: List which of your workflows depend on one model provider, and test a fallback model for the most important one.
Ask your Anthropic account team what capacity and rate limits your contract guarantees, in writing.
If you budget for AI, plan for prices and limits to move as providers balance compute against revenue.
stories.example: A support team that runs every ticket through Claude sets up a second provider for overflow, so a rate limit on a busy Monday slows replies instead of stopping them.
stories.audience: Teams that depend on Claude or any single AI provider, finance and procurement leads, and investors watching the IPO.
stories.watch: The final IPO price, expected 18 November, and first trading on 19 November. Any change to Claude rate limits or plans after the listing.

source.title: The Decoder: Anthropic CEO Amodei admits “there’s a huge uncertainty in what’s going to happen next year” days before a record IPO, 14 November 2026
source.quote: Speaking with JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon, he said, "Compute is the deepest business dilemma that the company faces."

stories.theme: A Japanese-led investigation found about 1,000 servers that appear to be bases for AI-driven cyberattacks on websites worldwide
stories.changed: On Saturday 14 November 2026 Kyodo News reported the results of an international investigation led by JPCERT/CC, Japan’s computer emergency response centre, working with overseas security firms. It found around 1,000 servers suspected of serving as bases for AI-driven cyberattacks, online since October. JPCERT/CC began investigating in early October and is tracking 600 to 700 of them. Most hosted AI-powered platforms such as the penetration-testing tool Artex, and appeared to be searching for weaknesses and trying to steal configuration files. One server held traces of an AI programming tool from Anthropic. Some held tools for taking apart smartphone apps and testing for weaknesses, and investigators believe attackers studied apps and then tried to break in through the interfaces those apps use to talk to outside systems. In October the Asahi Shimbun had reported that JPCERT/CC found files generated by Claude Code on attacker servers used against Japanese companies. JPCERT/CC analyst Ken Sajo warned that AI use in attacks is still early and that “more sophisticated attacks will increase in the future.”
stories.matters: Finding weak spots used to take skill and time. Automated, AI-driven scanning across hundreds of servers means small companies get probed as thoroughly as large ones.
stories.imply: Do not treat this as a Japan-only problem. The report says the servers targeted websites worldwide. Do not over-read the Anthropic trace either. The report does not say how much of the work AI did.
uses: List the APIs your mobile app talks to and check each one requires proper login and rate limits.
Search your web servers for configuration files, such as .env files, that anyone can download.
Ask your hosting or security provider whether it blocks automated vulnerability scanning.
stories.example: A retailer’s developer pulls apart its own Android app, finds an old API address still answering without a login, and switches it off the same afternoon.
stories.audience: Security and IT teams, developers of web and mobile apps, and small businesses with public websites.
stories.watch: Whether JPCERT/CC publishes a technical report with indicators to block. Whether AI tool makers respond to their tools showing up on attack servers.

source.title: The Straits Times (Kyodo News): Japan-led probe finds 1,000 servers likely used for AI-driven cyberattacks, 15 November 2026
source.quote: The probe by the Japan Computer Emergency Response Team Coordination Centre (JPCERT/CC), conducted in cooperation with overseas cybersecurity firms, found that the servers may have used AI to search for vulnerabilities and target websites worldwide.

stories.theme: IBM released small Granite models trained to obey only marked instructions and to ignore commands hidden in documents
stories.changed: On 12 November 2026 IBM released two experimental preview models, Granite 4.1 3B and 8B LLMON, with a toolkit on GitHub. LLMON, short for LLM Object Notation and pronounced “lemon”, is a markup in which each part of a prompt (an instruction, a piece of data, a requirement) sits in its own tagged block. The block edges are special tokens reserved in the model’s vocabulary, so text inside a document cannot pretend to be an instruction. A final block states which instruction to run, on which data. This targets indirect prompt injection, where an attacker hides a command in an email, web page or tool result. On the OPI benchmark IBM says the LLMON models avoided 47% more attacks than the best frontier model it tested and 95% more than the best open model, with similar results on two other benchmarks, and general ability on par with Granite 4.1 Instruct. You name the parts of a message and the bundled chat template does the rest; converters turn JSON into LLMON and back. IBM calls it a preview for exploration, not production, says the benchmarks test static attacks, and is still working on attacks that unfold over many turns.
stories.matters: Prompt injection is the main reason companies hesitate to let AI read outside email or web pages and then act. A model that tells instructions from data by design, rather than by a warning in its prompt, is a different kind of defence.
stories.imply: Do not drop your other safeguards. IBM says the resistance is learned, not guaranteed, and multi-turn attacks are untested. Do not put the preview into production.
uses: Run your own collection of injection attacks against the 8B preview and your current model, and compare.
Try it on a narrow job such as summarising inbound emails, where hidden instructions are a real risk.
Mark which parts of your existing prompts are instructions and which are data. It helps with any model.
stories.example: An IT team feeds 200 phishing emails containing hidden instructions to the 8B preview and to its current summariser, and counts how often each one follows the planted command.
stories.audience: Security teams, developers building agents that read untrusted content, and companies that want small models on their own servers.
stories.watch: Results against adaptive, multi-turn attacks. Whether IBM or others bring the approach to larger, production models.

source.title: Hugging Face (IBM Granite): LLMON: An LLM-Native Markup Language, now in Granite 4.1 3B and 8B, 12 November 2026
source.quote: This is a learned behavior, not an enforced guarantee.

stories.theme: llama.cpp, the engine for running AI models on your own hardware, reached version 1.0 with a promise not to break apps without warning
stories.changed: On Friday 13 November 2026 the ggml-org team at Hugging Face released llama.cpp v1.0.0 and ggml v1.0.0, three and a half years after the project began. llama.cpp lets people run language models, including ones that read images, on everything from laptops to servers. From now on the version number carries a promise: a major version (2.0) signals a breaking change to the public programming interface, a minor version adds backward-compatible features, hardware backends or model support, and a patch only fixes bugs. The team says it supports more than 150 model architecture variants and all mainstream speculative decoding methods. It is distributed through Docker, Debian, Homebrew, conda-forge, MacPorts, Winget and an Apple XCFramework, with builds for Linux, macOS, Windows, Android and iOS. Nvidia, AMD, Qualcomm, Arm, IBM and Intel provide hardware for its test machines.
stories.matters: Many local AI apps are built on llama.cpp. A stable interface makes running models on your own hardware cheaper to maintain, which matters for teams that cannot send data to the cloud.
stories.imply: Do not expect 1.0 to make a model smarter or faster on its own. It is a stability promise. If your app uses older functions, check the release notes before upgrading.
uses: If your product embeds llama.cpp, pin it to the 1.x line and plan upgrades around major versions only.
Install it through your usual package manager (Homebrew, Winget, Docker) instead of building from source.
Re-test a private, on-device AI use case you had shelved because the tooling kept changing.
stories.example: A law firm’s IT team installs llama.cpp through Winget on a few staff laptops to summarise documents offline, knowing a routine update will not break their setup.
stories.audience: Developers of local and on-device AI apps, IT teams with data that must stay in-house, and hobbyists.
stories.watch: How quickly downstream apps move to 1.x. What the first 1.x minor releases add.

source.title: Hugging Face (ggml-org): llama.cpp v1.0.0: A stronger foundation for the local AI ecosystem, 13 November 2026
source.quote: Moving forward, both llama.cpp and ggml will reflect API and ABI incompatibilities with major-version bumps.

stories.theme: OpenAI broke up its stand-alone robotics team, betting its general models can run robots directly
stories.changed: On Friday 13 November 2026 OpenAI confirmed to Fortune that it has disbanded its stand-alone robotics team. Robotics researchers now sit in the main research organisation under chief research officer Mark Chen, and the applied robotics and hardware teams moved to the Applied organisation under president Greg Brockman. The change was recent enough that OpenAI’s booth at the CoRL robotics conference in Austin sat empty. A spokesperson said robotics remains a core part of OpenAI’s long-term vision and that this is the fastest way to general-purpose robots. OpenAI said that at the start of the year it expected progress to come from video models like Sora, but that general models including GPT-6 Astra have shown they can be applied to robots directly. Fortune cites an Nvidia study where an Astra-powered agent scored 74.8% on a simulated manipulation benchmark, against 51.0% for the best specialised robot models. Fortune also notes OpenAI is under pressure to cut costs, with a reported $10.9 billion operating loss last quarter. Sam Altman still targets a first public humanoid demonstration in 2027.
stories.matters: If general models can drive robots, the same AI that writes your emails could run machines in a warehouse. That challenges robotics startups that raised money on the idea that robots need their own specialised brains.
stories.imply: Do not read a simulation score as factory readiness. Experts quoted by Fortune say small on-robot models are still needed, and that real deployment data stays valuable.
uses: If you are piloting robots, ask the vendor whether its edge is its own model or the data from real sites.
Keep data from your own robots and machines. Better general models make site-specific data more useful.
Treat 2027 humanoid timelines as a target, not a delivery date, in any planning.
stories.example: A logistics manager weighing two picking-robot vendors asks each how its robots learn from her warehouse, and who owns that data if she switches.
stories.audience: Operations and manufacturing leaders, robotics investors, and teams piloting robots.
stories.watch: OpenAI’s planned 2027 humanoid demonstration. Whether other labs fold robotics into general model teams.
